name: PC-PBT-CF (Carbon-Fiber-Filled PC/PBT Blend)
chemical_makeup: The same bisphenol-A polycarbonate / polybutylene terephthalate alloy as the pc-pbt grade — an amorphous PC phase for stiffness and heat, a semicrystalline PBT phase for solvent, oil and fuel resistance — compounded with chopped carbon fiber. The fiber loading is not disclosed by the one vendor selling this material.
summary: The low-warp, precision-oriented member of the PC family, and by some distance the cheapest fiber-filled engineering material in this catalog at roughly $57/kg. Deltas vs the pc-pbt grade: no heated chamber required, a much faster ceiling (up to 250 mm/s), and a manufacturer anti-warp claim — paid for with a mandatory hardened nozzle and the usual fiber penalty to layer adhesion. Tensile 60 MPa and a 2200 MPa modulus put it above the unfilled blend on stiffness. The published density of 1.01 g/cm³ is unusually low for a CF-filled blend and is recorded as-published rather than corrected.

printing.notes: Extrudr's DuraPro PC/PBT CF is the only product behind this entry: 265-295 °C nozzle, 100-110 °C bed, part cooling 0-30 %, speed to 250 mm/s. The most consequential delta against the unfilled pc-pbt grade is heated_chamber_required, which is false here where it is true there — Polymaker's unfilled grade specifies a maintained 100-110 °C chamber, while Extrudr publishes no chamber requirement for the filled one and markets it on low warp instead. An enclosure is still recommended. The 250 mm/s figure is a vendor ceiling for the material rather than a practical recommendation; 60 mm/s is a conservative working value and is not itself a published figure. Hardened nozzle mandatory — carbon fiber destroys brass.

feeding.notes: Rigid and stiff, so any drive system feeds it. AMS is 'conditional' rather than 'yes' on the usual fiber grounds: chopped carbon fiber abrades a PTFE feed path over time, and the PC phase wants a sealed desiccated route. No vendor documents this material in a material station (unverified). Unlike the unfilled pc-pbt grade, there is no 100-110 °C chamber for an AMS to sit next to, which removes the thermal objection.

drying.dryness_validation: Clear extrudate with no popping at the nozzle and no visible voids in a purge line. Extrudr publishes no explicit check for this grade (unverified) — these are the base PC-PBT criteria.
drying.notes: No drying schedule is published for the CF grade, so the unfilled pc-pbt regimen (75 °C / 6 h, itself carried from base PC) is applied here (unverified for this material specifically). The PC phase dominates moisture behaviour and fiber loading does not change that, so the carry-over is defensible.

storage.recommendations: Airtight container with desiccant; print from a drybox on long jobs. Follows base PC practice.

price.notes: Approximately $57/kg, derived from a $40.10 listing for a 700 g spool at 3DJake. That makes it the cheapest carbon-fiber-filled engineering material in this catalog by a wide margin — roughly half the price of the CF nylons and a third of ppa-cf. Single retailer, single spool size; the broader band is unverified.

recommended: precision industrial parts where dimensional repeatability matters
pulleys, rollers and other mechanically loaded rotating parts
low-warp structural parts at large footprints
jigs and fixtures exposed to oils and solvents
stiff brackets where unfilled PC-PBT would flex
not_recommended: cosmetic prints — the fiber-matte surface is not a finish
parts loaded in Z (fiber reinforcement worsens the anisotropy)
sustained outdoor UV exposure without coating
maximum-heat applications — service tops out around 130 °C

properties.notes: Density 1.01 g/cm³ is recorded exactly as Extrudr publishes it and is flagged rather than corrected: it is markedly below the unfilled pc-pbt grade's 1.20 g/cm³, which is the opposite direction from what a carbon-fiber loading normally produces, and it makes this the lightest engineering material in the catalog by volume (99 cm³ per 100 g). Treat it as a vendor figure requiring verification, and note that the derived weight/volume fields inherit the anomaly. HDT-B (1.8 MPa flexural) 85 °C; Vicat A 130 °C; the recorded 130 °C maximum service temperature rests on the Vicat figure rather than on a continuous-use rating, which overstates practical service under load — HDT-B 85 °C is the number to design to. Tensile 60 MPa with a tensile modulus of 2200 MPa, both above the unfilled blend's 50.4 MPa. Warp is described by the manufacturer as low, an anti-warp formulation claim rather than a measured shrinkage figure; no shrinkage percentage is published and none is recorded.

compatibility.notes: Welds to itself and, on shared PC chemistry, to the unfilled pc-pbt grade and the rest of the PC family — plausible from chemistry and inherited from the base entry rather than documented for the filled grade (unverified). HIPS is the practical breakaway support at these bed temperatures, carried from pc-pbt. pva degrades far below the 265-295 °C window; bvoh's stability through a long job at this temperature is unverified, so it is omitted as it is on the base entry. Not usable as a support for other materials — the melt window is too hot and the fiber-filled surface too aggressive.

alternatives.reason: The unfilled base: better layer adhesion (7 vs 5), no hardened nozzle, and a documented Polymaker datasheet behind its numbers — but it requires a maintained 100-110 °C chamber where the CF grade does not, and it gives up the stiffness (2200 MPa modulus) and the 60 MPa tensile.

Cheaper again and dramatically easier on ordinary hardware (no enclosure, ~240 °C nozzle) for stiff, dimensionally decent parts — giving up roughly 40 °C of heat resistance, the PBT phase's solvent and fuel resistance, and the PC phase's toughness.

Glass rather than carbon fiber on a PC base: comparable stiffness with better layer adhesion and none of the carbon dust hazard — but without the PBT phase it crazes in solvents and fuels where this blend does not.

emissions.notes: Carried from the unfilled pc-pbt entry, whose reasoning holds here: no styrene, so the VOC profile follows base PC's 'moderate', while particulates are 'high' because a 265-295 °C nozzle inside a warm enclosure concentrates ultrafine particles that escape when the door opens. The addition over the unfilled grade is post-processing carbon fiber dust. No measurement covers this material (unverified) — vent or filter, and let the enclosure clear before opening.

safety_notes: Abrasive: a hardened steel or ruby nozzle is mandatory and brass will not survive a spool. Wear respiratory protection with dust capture when sanding or machining printed parts — carbon fiber fines are a respiratory irritant. Bisphenol-A based like every PC grade, so keep parts away from food and drink regardless of surface finish. The 265-295 °C hotend and 110 °C bed are burn hazards and the enclosure concentrates off-gassing.
additional_notes: Two figures on this entry deserve scepticism before anything is designed around them. The published density of 1.01 g/cm³ runs the wrong way for a fiber-filled blend and is recorded as-published. The 130 °C service figure rests on a Vicat A softening point, not a continuous-use rating; the HDT-B of 85 °C is the realistic design number under load. Set against that, the price is genuinely remarkable for a CF-filled engineering material, and the removal of the base grade's heated-chamber requirement makes it the only member of the PC-PBT family that prints on ordinary enclosed hardware.

provenance.conflicts: Single-vendor entry — Extrudr DuraPro PC/PBT CF is the only product found, so nothing here is corroborated by a second source. Density 1.01 g/cm³ is the standout oddity: it is well below the unfilled pc-pbt grade's 1.20 and runs contrary to the expected effect of a carbon-fiber loading, which normally raises density. It is recorded as-published and flagged; the derived weight/volume fields inherit the anomaly. Maximum service temperature of 130 °C is taken from the Vicat A softening point rather than a continuous-use rating, and sits well above the HDT-B figure of 85 °C measured at 1.8 MPa — the two describe different things and the Vicat basis is noted rather than reconciled. Low warp is a manufacturer anti-warp formulation claim, not a measured shrinkage figure, and the warp_tendency score of 4 rests on that claim. Fiber loading percentage is not disclosed. Price is derived from a single 700 g spool listing ($40.10) at one retailer. Drying schedule, bonding pairs, shrinkage and AMS status are all carried from the unfilled pc-pbt entry rather than published for this grade.

trade_names.notes: The only product behind this entry: 265-295 °C nozzle, 100-110 °C bed, density 1.01 g/cm3, HDT-B 85 °C, Vicat A 130 °C, tensile 60 MPa / modulus 2200 MPa. Fiber loading not disclosed.
